title: New Fossil Trove Redefines Earth’s “Big Five” Mass Extinction Narrative, Scientists Say
body:
A new artificial‑intelligence analysis of almost four million fossil specimens is reshaping the narrative of Earth’s most dramatic biodiversity crises. By feeding a massive dataset into a machine‑learning model, researchers have uncovered evidence that three of the five traditionally recognized “big five” mass‑extinction events unfolded over much longer intervals than the abrupt, cataclysmic spikes long held by paleontologists. The findings, published this week, suggest that the Permian‑Triassic, Late Devonian and end‑Cretaceous die‑offs may have been protracted, multi‑phased processes rather than single, instantaneous catastrophes.

The team employed a deep‑learning framework that can detect subtle patterns in the temporal and taxonomic distribution of fossils. By training the algorithm on a curated collection of roughly 3.9 million records—spanning marine invertebrates, vertebrates, plants and microfossils—the model generated high‑resolution extinction curves that reveal the tempo of biodiversity loss with unprecedented detail. In contrast to conventional methods that rely on manually compiled stratigraphic ranges, the AI‑driven approach can interpolate gaps, correct for sampling bias and integrate disparate data sources, producing a more continuous picture of how species numbers fluctuated through deep time.

When the model’s output was compared with the classic textbook view, striking discrepancies emerged. The Permian‑Triassic event, often dubbed “the Great Dying” and thought to have eradicated up to 96 % of marine species within a few hundred thousand years, instead appears to have begun a full million years before the traditionally defined boundary and to have progressed in several pulses. Similarly, the Late Devonian crisis, previously characterized as a relatively brief interval of reef collapse and vertebrate loss, shows a drawn‑out decline extending over several million years, punctuated by episodic spikes that align with known volcanic and sea‑level fluctuations. Perhaps most surprising is the end‑Cretaceous extinction, famously linked to the Chicxulub impact that wiped out the non‑avian dinosaurs. The AI analysis indicates a gradual downturn in dinosaur diversity beginning several hundred thousand years before the impact, suggesting that ecological stressors—such as climate change and sea‑level regression—may have already weakened ecosystems before the asteroid struck.

These revelations have far‑reaching implications for how scientists interpret the drivers of mass extinctions. If extinction events are more protracted, it becomes plausible that multiple, interacting mechanisms—volcanism, ocean anoxia, climate perturbations, and extraterrestrial impacts—worked in concert over extended periods, rather than a single, dominant trigger. This nuanced view could reconcile long‑standing debates, such as the relative importance of the Siberian Traps eruptions versus rapid warming in the Permian, or the role of Deccan flood basalts alongside the Chicxulub impact at the end of the Cretaceous. Moreover, the study underscores the growing utility of big‑data analytics in paleobiology, where traditional fieldwork is complemented by computational tools capable of sifting through terabytes of fossil information.

Critics caution that AI models are only as good as the data they ingest, and fossil records are inherently incomplete and unevenly distributed across time and space. The authors acknowledge these limitations, emphasizing that the algorithm is designed to highlight patterns rather than replace rigorous stratigraphic work. Nonetheless, the ability to quantify extinction rates with finer temporal resolution opens new avenues for testing hypotheses about cause‑and‑effect relationships in Earth’s deep past.

Looking ahead, the research team plans to expand the dataset to include more terrestrial and soft‑tissue fossils, as well as isotopic and geochemical proxies, to refine the extinction timelines further. By integrating climate models and tectonic reconstructions, future studies could simulate how gradual environmental stresses compounded to push ecosystems past tipping points. As the planet confronts a sixth mass extinction driven by human activity, understanding the tempo and complexity of past crises may offer crucial lessons for predicting and potentially averting future biodiversity collapses.
